title: Stratus Edu - model selection, context & tool-calling discovery
summary: Initial discovery to understand Stratus Education Labs' needs for grading/feedback assistant across multilingual student submissions. Key topics: open model comparisons (privacy-sensitive), long context needs for full student essays (~20-25k tokens), function/tool calling for rubric-based grading, hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment (on-prem for some customers), SOC 2/KMS requirements, latency vs throughput trade-offs. Agreed next steps: run a 2-week PoC on Redwood Dedicated with a 32k context variant, share security pack and cost estimate, schedule technical deep-dive for infra team.
topics: deployment modes: hosted vs dedicated vs private
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-06-25 15:00 UTC
Duration: 49 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: Enabled
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE); Ethan (Redwood SE); Janelle (Redwood CSM, joined late); Dr. Lina Morales (CTO); Samir Patel (ML Eng); Aisha Khan (Infra); Jordan Lee (Product)

--- Auto-summary (auto-generated):
Stratus is building an automated grading assistant that needs long context to analyze full essays, multilingual understanding, and deterministic rubric tooling. They are leaning toward Dedicated or Private due to data residency and on-prem partner contracts but want cost comparison vs Hosted. They requested security docs and a benchmark plan.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, I'm Maya, AE at Redwood. Quick roll call?
[00:12] Dr. Morales: Lina here, hi.
[00:14] Samir: Samir present.
[00:15] Aisha: Aisha.
[00:16] Jordan: Jordan, product.
[00:18] Ethan (Redwood SE): Ethan, Redwood SE.
[00:20] Maya: Great. Our goal today is high level discovery on models, context length, and how tool-calling might fit into your grading flow. Samir, can you start with the current architecture?
[00:30] Samir: Sure, so right now we have a microservice that pulls student submissions from our storage, we pre-process, then we call a third-party API for summarization and some heuristic scoring. The problem is the third-party cuts off at 8k tokens and we lose essay context, especially with attachments and inline citations. We want a single inference runtime that can take the whole essay plus rubric and previous feedback — often 15 to 25k tokens.
[01:02] Maya: Got it. So you're assuming long context, likely 20k plus. On our side, we support models and runtime variants with 8k, 32k, and 64k context profiles. For the size you described I'd recommend testing the 32k profile first unless you have heavy multimodal attachments.
[01:25] Dr. Morales: Do you have open models that do well on multilingual grading? We have Spanish and Arabic cohorts and sometimes Chinese. Accuracy matters and we need low hallucination when scoring rubric items.
[01:38] Ethan: We maintain a catalog of vetted open models. For multilingual tasks, we often suggest variants of Mistral and Llama-2/3-based models that have been finetuned or instruction-tuned for multilingual. We also test Redwood-verified profiles that balance latency and cost. Quick caveat — some open models are stronger in certain languages, so we'd run a language-wise eval.
[02:04] Jordan: Can you do tool-calling? We need deterministic rubric evaluation — ideally the model returns structured fields for each rubric category plus a confidence score and references to exact essay offsets.
[02:17] Ethan: Yep, function-calling / structured output is a core use case. You can design a schema: rubric items, scores, comments, offsets. We can implement a strict parser and validation step in the pipeline. In Dedicated/Private modes we can add a second-step verifier to enforce determinism.
[02:36] Samir: On determinism — if we quantize models to reduce cost, do we see variance in outputs? We have to be careful since grades are user-facing.
[02:47] Ethan: Quantization can introduce some variability, especially aggressive 4-bit stacks. For rubric scoring, we recommend calibrated prompts and optionally running a small ensemble or majority-vote on a small sample. Dedicated instances let you pin kernel/compilation choices to limit drift.
[03:05] Aisha: For our schools, data residency and customer contracts require us to keep PII on-prem for some clients. How mature is Redwood Private for on-prem?
[03:18] Maya: Our Private deployment supports a customer-managed control plane with on-prem inference nodes. It's used by a number of customers with similar constraints. There's an on-prem package that bundles the runtime, orchestration, and a thin control plane. We also support VPC options for cloud-hosted private setups.
[03:35] Dr. Morales: What's the timeline to spin up Private vs Dedicated? We have a Q3 pilot date.
[03:41] Maya: Dedicated can be provisioned in a couple weeks with reserved capacity. Private on-prem varies — usually 6 to 10 weeks for full delivery and validation, depending on networking and compliance reviews. For your Q3 pilot, Dedicated or Hosted Dedicated with strict E2E controls is a common path.
[04:00] Jordan: Latency is important for our live feedback UI, but batch grading overnight is okay for official grades. We care about tail latency under 200-300ms for short interactions and throughput for nightly jobs.
[04:13] Ethan: For short interactions you can route to smaller, faster model variants. We support smart routing policies so UI calls go to low-latency variants and batch jobs use higher-context, more expensive variants. That reduces unit cost while meeting SLAs.
[04:29] Samir: Can we run a mix — like host the UI on Redwood Hosted for latency and keep grading on Dedicated or Private?
[04:36] Maya: Absolutely, hybrid routing is one of our strengths. Policy-based routing can send requests based on path, model, or customer tier.
[04:44] [05:00] Ethan: Quick note on caching — for revision flows we can cache prefix embeddings and KV caches for repeated student drafts which lowers token cost. Not perfect if essays change a lot, but can help.
[05:16] Dr. Morales: Security — we need SOC 2, SSO (SAML), RBAC, and KMS integration. Also audit logs for each inference request.
[05:26] Maya: We provide SOC 2 Type II docs, support SAML/SCIM for provisioning, RBAC, and KMS/HSM integrations. We also emit per-request audit logs with token-level cost breakdowns in the console. We'll share the security pack after this call.
[05:45] Jordan: Competitors — any concerns about OpenAI policy or cost? We're evaluating them and some self-host options.
[05:52] Maya: We see OpenAI for quick TTV; cost can be higher at scale and data residency is harder. Self-host gives control but higher ops overhead. Redwood tries to hit a middle: managed runtime + private options.
[06:06] Samir: On benchmarking — what would you suggest for our PoC? We want to test multilingual precision on rubric items, output structure fidelity, and end-to-end latency/cost.
[06:20] Ethan: We'll set up an eval harness. Typical plan: 1) small labeled set (200 essays across languages) for precision/recall on rubric fields; 2) throughput test for nightly batch (X essays/hour); 3) live UI latency test for short prompts. We'll include 8k vs 32k context models and compare outputs. We'll produce a benchmark spreadsheet.
[06:45] Dr. Morales: Are there known open-models that specifically excel at grading-style tasks?
[06:51] Ethan: There isn't a one-size-fits-all. We often start with instruction-tuned variants of Llama-3 and Mistral for English and Spanish, and BLOOM or multilingual optimized models for hard languages, then fine-tune or instruction-tune on your rubric. We can also do a small supervised fine-tune if you provide labeled examples.
[07:15] Aisha: For Private on-prem, what's the hardware profile? We have an internal GPU pool but need guidance on GPUs per instance for 32k context models.
[07:25] Ethan: For 32k context on 7B-ish models you can run on A100/RTX-8000 equipped nodes with 80GB memory per GPU and sharded setups. For larger models 13B+ we recommend multi-GPU / model parallel. We'll provide sizing guidance tailored to your expected concurrency.
[07:49] Samir: How about cost? We need a rough per-essay cost to compare with our current third-party vendor.
[07:57] Maya: We'll put together a cost estimate: token cost per model variant + infra + reserved capacity math for Dedicated. For Hosted we'll give per-token pricing estimates and for Dedicated a monthly reserved commitment example. We'll add a per-essay example based on an average essay length you give us.
[08:20] Jordan: Tool-calling specifics — we want the model to call an external 'plagiarism-check' tool and a 'citation-extract' function. Can Redwood route those calls to our internal services?
[08:33] Ethan: Yes, Redwood's function-calling supports tool integrations. In Dedicated/Private you can wire internal endpoints directly. For Hosted we support secure webhooks and encrypted transport. We'll help with example connectors.
[08:50] Dr. Morales: Any nuance around multilingual tokenization affecting context counts?
[08:56] Ethan: Good point — languages with denser tokenization (e.g., Chinese) change token counts. We'll include language-specific token estimates in the benchmark. For exact counts we run a tokenization pass on sample essays.
[09:12] [09:30] Janelle (Redwood CSM): Sorry I'm late — joining now.
[09:33] Maya: No worries. Janelle will coordinate the PoC timeline.
[09:38] Janelle: Great, I can own scheduling and onboarding.
[09:40] Samir: Are there guardrails for hallucinations? When the model fabricates a citation it's a big problem.
[09:47] Ethan: Two levers: grounding via retrieval (bring exact text snippets from the student's submitted attachments or external refs), and strict output parsing with verification. You can also penalize generation for 'unknown' citations and have the verifier flag them.
[10:07] Dr. Morales: For evaluation — we want F1 on rubric categories and a human-in-the-loop review threshold. Can Redwood support a hybrid workflow where low-confidence ones are queued for human graders?
[10:20] Maya: Absolutely. We can attach a confidence metric and route to human graders via your LMS integration.
[10:28] Jordan: Sizing pilot — what's a minimal starter PoC we can run quickly?
[10:33] Ethan: Start with 200 labeled essays (4 languages) and a 2-week Dedicated trial where we provision a small pool. We'll run the eval harness and share results. This will surface model gaps and allow prompt/tuning.
[10:48] Samir: Can we try prompt engineering first before any fine-tuning?
[10:52] Ethan: Yes, prompt/template iterations often yield large wins and are lower friction. We'll include prompt baseline tests in the benchmark plan.
[11:03] Aisha: Networking question — for Private, we need firewall whitelists and a proxy architecture. Is there a standard playbook?
[11:12] Maya: We have a deployment runbook for on-prem with example firewall rules and proxy configs. We'll share it and pair with your infra during the deep-dive.
[11:24] Dr. Morales: Any regulatory concerns? We operate globally so data residency and student privacy laws matter.
[11:29] Maya: We'll map requirements. For PII we recommend Dedicated or Private with KMS-managed keys and audit logs. We also support data redaction hooks in the ingest pipeline.
[11:44] Jordan: Competitor note — if we go with OpenAI for UI speed, we lose ability to pin model versions. Redwood's Dedicated sounds promising for grade determinism.
[11:54] Maya: That's the tradeoff. We can show a hybrid route again.
[12:00] [12:20] Ethan: Quick demo offer — would you like a focused technical deep-dive next week with your infra and ML teams to walk through sizing and a sample benchmark run?
[12:31] Dr. Morales: Yes, please. Next week works — ideally Tues or Wed.
[12:36] Maya: Noted. We'll coordinate via Janelle.
[12:40] Samir: One more ops question — how are model upgrades handled? We need to freeze model versions mid-semester.
[12:47] Ethan: You can pin versions per route and do canary rollouts. Dedicated gives you stronger control; Private brings full control. Rollouts are configurable in the console.
[12:58] Dr. Morales: OK we have enough. Thanks everyone.
[13:03] Maya: Quick recap: Redwood to send security pack, pricing for Hosted/Dedicated/Private, a proposed PoC plan (200 essays, 2-week Dedicated trial), benchmark spreadsheet template, and schedule deep-dive next week. Janelle will coordinate.
[13:20] Jordan: Thanks, bye.
[13:22] Maya: Thanks all.
